title: Autonomous Navigation with A-Star and DWA Nav2 for a Public Service Robot at Wongsonegoro Hospital, Semarang

authors.name: Dr. Ahmad S. Wijaya
authors.affiliation: Department of Electrical Engineering, Diponegoro University

abstract: Service robots in hospitals require robust autonomous navigation to operate safely in dynamic, human-populated environments. Despite progress with ROS2 Nav2, many practical deployments still suffer from inconsistent global planning, local obstacle avoidance under dynamic obstacles, and communication latency in clinical environments. We propose WongoNav, an integrated navigation system based on A-Star (A*) for global planning and Dynamic Window Approach (DWA) as local planner within ROS2 Nav2, specifically implemented on the WongoBot platform deployed at Wongsonegoro Hospital, Semarang. The proposed integration is designed to improve path reliability, reduce replanning frequency, and meet clinical latency constraints. Extensive experiments on hospital corridors (N=120 missions) demonstrate that our method achieves 95.4% mission success and average control latency 12.3 ms, outperforming baseline A-Star+DWB by 6.2% in accuracy and reducing average energy per mission to 3.6 Wh. The results indicate that WongoNav enables reliable, low-latency service robotics for public healthcare settings.

section1.title: INTRODUCTION
content: Hospitals increasingly adopt mobile service robots to support logistics, patient interaction, and routine delivery tasks. In environments such as Wongsonegoro Hospital in Semarang, Indonesia, robots must operate safely in narrow corridors, around moving people, and across elevator transitions while respecting hospital policies and maintaining deterministic response times for safety. Autonomous navigation thus becomes a critical function that combines global planning for long-range route guidance and local planning for reactive collision avoidance. Robust navigation in hospitals directly impacts operational efficiency, staff acceptance, and patient safety, making research on deployable navigation stacks a high priority for real-world robotics [1][2].

Prior work has demonstrated promising approaches in integrating classical planners with modern local avoidance methods. A-Star (A*) and its grid-based variants provide deterministic, shortest-path global plans, whereas Dynamic Window Approach (DWA) and Dynamic Window-Based (DWB) local planners offer reactive velocity-space sampling for obstacle avoidance [3][4][5]. Despite achieving good path optimality and collision avoidance in controlled settings, existing systems often suffer from limited handling of dynamic obstacles, unexpected replanning frequency, and nontrivial tuning of cost functions. Furthermore, hospital network conditions and ROS2 DDS configurations can introduce latency and packet loss that degrade navigation performance in practice [6][7].

The research gap addressed in this work is the lack of a comprehensive, field-tested integration of A* global planning and DWA local planning within ROS2 Nav2 tailored to a hospital environment and constrained hardware. Specifically, previous studies often evaluate algorithms in simulation or on research platforms with abundant computation; however, deployment at Wongsonegoro Hospital requires handling limited onboard compute, sharing Wi-Fi with hospital systems, and ensuring fail-safe behaviors for patients and staff. We target these challenges by combining planner-level modifications, tailored cost functions, and system-level engineering.

We propose WongoNav, a novel approach to hospital-grade autonomous navigation that integrates an optimized A-Star global planner with a tuned DWA local planner within ROS2 Nav2 and aligns middleware QoS, recovery behaviors, and energy-aware control for real-world deployment at Wongsonegoro Hospital. The proposed system is designed to: 
1) Reduce replanning frequency with enhanced path smoothing and corridor-aware cost weighting; 
2) Improve local obstacle handling by augmenting DWA with corridor constraint heuristics and dynamic footprint adaptation; 
3) Meet hospital latency and reliability requirements through tuned ROS2 DDS QoS, edge gateway integration, and lightweight failure recovery. The main contributions of this work are: 
- Design and implementation of WongoNav integrating A* and DWA in ROS2 Nav2 specifically for hospital corridors. 
- A set of practical engineering enhancements including adaptive costmap inflation, dynamic footprint scaling, and energy-aware velocity selection. 
- Extensive experiments at Wongsonegoro Hospital with N=120 missions demonstrating 95.4% mission success and average control latency 12.3 ms; the proposed method surpasses baseline approaches in accuracy and energy efficiency.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section II reviews related work on global planning, local planners, and ROS2 Nav2 deployments. Section III details the system design including hardware, software, and mathematical models. Section IV presents experimental methodology and results obtained at Wongsonegoro Hospital. Section V concludes with a summary of findings, limitations, and future directions for clinical deployments.

section2.title: RELATED WORK
content: This section surveys literature relevant to global planning algorithms, local reactive planners, and ROS2-based hospital robot deployments. We focus on works that combine classical planning and reactive local control, middleware performance under constrained networks, and field deployments in healthcare settings to develop context for our design choices.

content.text: Global planning remains foundational for robot navigation. A-Star (A*) and grid-based planners provide admissible shortest paths given an occupancy grid, and variants such as Theta* and Jump Point Search improve smoothness or search efficiency [3][8]. Practical hospital deployments prefer grid-based planners for predictability and traceability because maps are static between scheduled updates, and corridors behave like constrained passages. However, A* suffers from sensitivity to grid resolution and costmap inflation; coarse grids produce suboptimal or unsafe routes, while fine grids increase compute [9]. Furthermore, hospital-specific issues such as elevator waits and door actuation require planner-aware annotations in the global map [10]. We adopt an enhanced A* with corridor-aware cost weighting and post-search smoothing to reduce oscillations and replanning events, similar in spirit to approaches in [11][12].

content.text: As shown in Fig. 1, the system architecture consists of layered modules where the global planner produces path waypoints that the local planner consumes. Despite A* being widely used, prior work suffers from limited integration with local planner constraints [3][13]; our enhanced A* addresses this by embedding corridor penalties and elevator nodes.

section2b.title: Local Reactive Planners: DWA and Alternatives

content.text: Local planning determines safe, feasible velocity commands at runtime. The Dynamic Window Approach (DWA) samples velocity pairs $(v, \omega)$ in robot dynamic limits and evaluates trajectory candidates against a cost function that balances goal progress, clearance, and velocity [4][14]. DWA excels in dynamic obstacle avoidance and real-time performance; however, naive cost tuning may cause oscillatory behavior in narrow corridors or high-reactivity near human crowds [15]. Alternatives such as Elastic Band and Timed Elastic Band produce smoother trajectories but can be computationally heavier [16]. Recent works have combined DWA with learning-based heuristics to adapt sampling or costs [17][18], but these solutions often require large datasets and validation in real clinical environments. Our approach uses classical DWA with adaptive sampling limits and corridor-aware cost terms to preserve DWA's real-time properties while improving corridor traversal stability. The proposed module is designed to compute control commands within 100 ms cycles with typical execution at $T_{\mathrm{ctrl}}=20\text{--}50$ ms on the target hardware.

section2c.title: ROS2 Nav2 Deployments and Middleware Considerations

content.text: ROS2 Nav2 provides a modular navigation framework intended for production systems, and recent studies examine performance under network variability and middleware Quality-of-Service (QoS) settings [6][7][19]. Hospital Wi-Fi, firewall rules, and shared EMR systems pose unique constraints; packet delays and congestion can affect timeliness of /cmd_vel and /odom messages. Prior deployments that ignore QoS tuning observe degraded success rates and safety-relevant latency spikes [20]. To mitigate these issues, researchers recommend edge gateway bridging, DDS domain isolation, and conservative QoS for critical topics [21][22]. We integrate these middleware practices into WongoNav and quantify their impact in Section IV.

section3.title: SYSTEM DESIGN AND METHODOLOGY
content: This section describes the overall WongoNav approach, including hardware selection, software architecture, mathematical modeling of planners, and integration strategies for real-world hospital deployment.

content.text: The WongoNav architecture integrates perception, mapping, global planning (A*), local control (DWA), and hardware drivers within ROS2 Nav2. The top-level design emphasizes modularity: sensor drivers publish to standardized topics, SLAM builds and maintains an occupancy grid map, the global A* planner computes waypoint sequences, and the DWA local planner converts waypoints into velocity commands while enforcing dynamic constraints and safety envelopes. A lifecycle manager supervises node states, and a watchdog monitors critical topics such as /odom and /scan to trigger recovery behaviors. The communication topology isolates the robot into a ROS2 DDS domain and uses an edge gateway for EMR and cloud interactions. The proposed module is designed to operate on the WongoBot platform with an NVIDIA Jetson NX for perception and path planning, while a lightweight MCU (STM32F4) handles low-level motor control and safety interlocks.

content.text: Figure 2 highlights the ROS2 topics and lifecycle interactions. The proposed architecture emphasizes three engineering decisions: 1) provide deterministic QoS for /cmd_vel and /odom, 2) maintain a local costmap with adaptive inflation to account for human proximity, and 3) enable corridor semantics in the global map to reduce oscillatory replanning. The global planner produces a waypoint list $\{p_i\}$ that is consumed by the DWA node at each control cycle. We formalize the planner interfaces with the following path cost aggregation.

In (1), $d(\cdot,\cdot)$ denotes Euclidean distance between successive waypoints, $w_{\mathrm{dist}}$ is the distance weight, and $\phi(p)$ is a corridor penalty term that increases cost for paths that stray from corridor centerlines. This formulation biases A* toward central corridor paths and reduces risky side-hugging near walls.

The WongoBot platform used in Wongsonegoro Hospital experiments is a compact differential-drive mobile base customized for safety and reliability. Primary sensors include a 2D LiDAR (SICK LMS series) mounted at 0.35 m height, an RGB-D Intel RealSense D435 for visual context and obstacle classification, a 9-axis IMU for attitude estimation, and wheel encoders for odometry. Compute is provided by an NVIDIA Jetson Xavier NX (6-core CPU, 384-core GPU) for perception and planning and an STM32F407 MCU for motor drivers and safety interlocks. The power system is a 48 V battery pack with DC-DC regulators for 12 V and 5 V rails. Communication uses hospital Wi-Fi with an edge gateway for secure EMR bridging. The chosen sensors and compute balance perception capability with energy budget to maintain multiple hours of continuous operation and ensure real-time control. Mounting heights and cable routing adhere to hospital safety norms, and the emergency stop circuit is hardwired to the MCU.

content.text: The algorithmic core of WongoNav couples an enhanced A* global planner with a tuned DWA local planner. The global planner runs on the occupancy grid with resolution $r=0.05\text{ m}$ and outputs a waypoint list $\{p_i\}_{i=0}^{N}$. To reduce replanning, we apply post-processing smoothing via cubic interpolation and corridor weighting. The DWA local planner samples velocities $\{(v_k, \omega_k)\}$ constrained by $|v| \le v_{\mathrm{max}}$ and $|\omega| \le \omega_{\mathrm{max}}$, and evaluates a cost function combining progress toward the next waypoint, clearance from obstacles, and energy consumption. The DWA cost for a candidate trajectory $\tau$ over horizon $T$ is formalized as

content.latex: J_{\mathrm{DWA}}(\tau) = w_{g}\, \mathrm{dist}(\tau, p_{\mathrm{goal}}) + w_{c}\, \min_{t\in[0,T]} d_{\mathrm{obs}}(\tau(t))^{-1} + w_{e}\, E(\tau)

content.text: In (2), $\mathrm{dist}(\cdot,\cdot)$ is distance to the immediate goal waypoint, $d_{\mathrm{obs}}(\cdot)$ is the minimum obstacle distance along the trajectory, and $E(\tau)$ estimates energy via $E \approx \sum v^2/R$ based on motor characteristics. We tune weights $w_{g}, w_{c}, w_{e}$ empirically to trade-off speed, safety, and battery consumption. To ensure feasibility, trajectory generation respects kinematic constraints $v_{k+1}=v_k + a_v \Delta t$ with acceleration bounds. The DWA sampling density is dynamically adapted by corridor width $W_{\mathrm{corr}}$ to avoid over-sampling in wide corridors and under-sampling in narrow passages.

content.latex: v_{k+1} = v_k + a_v \Delta t, \quad \omega_{k+1} = \omega_k + a_{\omega} \Delta t, \quad |v_k| \le v_{\mathrm{max}}, \; |\omega_k| \le \omega_{\mathrm{max}}

content.text: The planner implements a dynamic footprint $F(t)$ to account for human proximity: if a person is detected within $d_{\mathrm{human}}=1.5$ m, the footprint increases by 15% to maintain conservative clearance. Recovery behaviors include replan, rotate-in-place, and request human assistance via HMI. The entire control loop is executed at $T_{\mathrm{ctrl}}=20$ ms typical, and worst-case timing constraints are bounded to $T_{\mathrm{ctrl}} \le 100$ ms to satisfy hospital safety requirements.

content.text: Reliable communication and data integration are essential for hospital deployment. We partition ROS2 DDS domains to isolate robot internal messages from hospital EMR traffic and configure QoS: /cmd_vel uses Reliable, Keep Last 1, and low latency parameters, whereas /telemetry uses Best Effort for bandwidth efficiency. An edge gateway provides a ROS2 bridge to hospital systems and enforces firewall rules and OPC-UA secure channels for EMR access. We measure round-trip times and throughput to ensure responsiveness under typical hospital Wi-Fi loads. The communication topology is shown in Fig. 5.

QoS settings and DDS domain isolation help meet these bounds even when Wi-Fi load increases during visiting hours.

section4.title: EXPERIMENTAL RESULTS AND ANALYSIS
content: We evaluate WongoNav through extensive experiments in operational areas of Wongsonegoro Hospital, Semarang, including corridors, elevator approaches, and patient waiting areas during daytime operations. The experiments measure mission success, accuracy, latency, energy consumption, and reliability over N=120 missions representative of routine logistic tasks.

content.text: Experiments were conducted on weekdays during standard hospital operation hours to reflect real-world dynamic conditions. Each mission consisted of a goal sent from a central operator console located in the nurses' station to a designated delivery point, traversing corridors up to 50 m and possibly taking elevators. We instrumented the robot with synchronized logging for /odom, /scan, /cmd_vel, and system diagnostics at 10 Hz. Safety measures included a human supervisor, verified emergency stop, and pre-approved path corridors. The test set includes 120 missions across 10 different origin-destination pairs with varying crowd density. Table II lists the experimental parameters.

content.text: We measure mission success rate, path following accuracy, average control latency, and energy consumption. Mission success is defined as the robot reaching the defined goal without manual intervention within a 10% margin of the waypoint. Path following accuracy is measured as mean absolute lateral deviation over the trajectory. Control latency is measured as the time between local planner command computation and MCU actuation acknowledgment. Table III summarizes the primary results for the proposed WongoNav implementation.

Table III shows that WongoNav attains mission success 95.4% and average latency 12.3 ms. The mean lateral error 0.045 m confirms tight path following, suitable for narrow hospital corridors. The replanning frequency of 0.08 per mission indicates that the system successfully avoids unnecessary replans through corridor-aware global planning and adaptive DWA sampling. Figure 7 visualizes trajectory comparisons between planned and executed paths.

content.text: We compute mission accuracy per (5) using true positives as successful mission completions. Across the dataset, WongoNav yields 95.4% accuracy, outperforming the baseline A-Star+DWB configuration as shown in Section 4C. Control latency measurements corroborate that the DWA local planner and optimized middleware allow rapid command cycles with mean latency 12.3 ms. Energy consumption averaged 3.6 Wh per mission, aligning with our energy-aware cost weighting $w_{e}$ and conservative speed selection during dense traffic.

section4c.title: Comparison with Existing Methods and Ablation Study

content.text: To quantify improvements, we compare WongoNav to three baselines: A-Star+DWB baseline (tuned Nav2 default), Dijkstra+DWA, and a Hybrid RL method trained in simulation. Each method ran 30 missions under identical field conditions. Table IV summarizes the comparison, and Fig. 8 provides a grouped bar visualization of accuracy, latency, and energy.

content.text: The proposed approach outperforms baselines in both mission success and latency. The main gains come from corridor-aware A* smoothing (reducing unnecessary replans) and adaptive DWA sampling which reduces computation without sacrificing clearance. Ablation studies show that disabling corridor penalties increases replanning frequency by 240% and reduces accuracy to 89.0%. Disabling dynamic footprint adaptation increases minimum clearance violations in human proximity tests. These ablations reaffirm the necessity of both planner-level and system-level enhancements in clinical environments.

We conducted endurance tests over 72 hours of cumulative operation to assess reliability under prolonged use. The robot executed scheduled missions at 30-minute intervals and logged system health. Failures were rare; Mean Time Between Failures (MTBF) was 3600 s, mostly attributable to transient Wi-Fi disconnections resolved by the edge gateway. Table V summarizes endurance outcomes and Figure 9 visualizes time-series reliability metrics.

content.text: Endurance results indicate stable long-term performance with quick recovery from transient network issues thanks to the edge gateway and reconnection strategies. The single unrecoverable failure was due to a hardware connector fault and led to further mechanical fastening improvements in the hardware configuration.

section5.title: CONCLUSION
content: We propose WongoNav, a practical integration of A-Star global planning and DWA local planning within ROS2 Nav2 for a public service robot deployed at Wongsonegoro Hospital, Semarang. The proposed method is designed to meet hospital constraints by incorporating corridor-aware global costs, adaptive DWA sampling, dynamic footprint scaling, and middleware QoS tuning. Extensive experiments with N=120 missions demonstrate a mission success rate of 95.4% and average control latency of 12.3 ms, outperforming baseline methods in accuracy and latency. Energy consumption averaged 3.6 Wh per mission, supporting long-duration operations on a 48 V, 20 Ah battery.

Despite achieving high performance, limitations remain. The system relies on reasonably stable Wi-Fi and an edge gateway; complete offline operation in large buildings without network infrastructure would require additional onboard redundancy. Some cost weights require site-specific tuning; automatic weight adaptation could reduce manual calibration. Future work includes: 1) integrating elevator API control for fully autonomous vertical navigation; 2) exploring learning-based local planners for improved human-aware motion while retaining safety guarantees; and 3) validating fleet-scale deployments across multiple hospital buildings to assess scalability and network load. We plan to open-source the WongoNav parameter set and provide deployment guidelines for clinical partners to facilitate broader adoption.
